Folklore of India: folk tales, epics, songs and performers

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Indian folklore is the body of traditions that people pass on by word of mouth and example: folk tales, oral epics, songs, riddles, proverbs, festivals, crafts and beliefs. It exists in every Indian language and community, and is carried by both ordinary families and specialist performers such as the bhopas of Rajasthan and Pandavani singers of Chhattisgarh.

We run an oral history lab and a storytelling studio that teach students to record and retell folklore with care, online or in person.

What folklore means

Folklore is the traditional knowledge and art that people learn from each other informally rather than from books or schools. The term was coined in English in 1846, but the material it describes is as old as speech. Folklorists usually include oral forms such as tales, songs, proverbs and riddles; customary forms such as festivals, rituals and games; and material forms such as crafts, house decoration and food.

Folklore is not only rural, old or fading. City children have playground rhymes, office workers share jokes and stories, and new forms appear all the time. What makes something folklore is that it lives in variation: every teller changes a story a little, and no single version is the correct one. This makes folklore a close relative of intangible cultural heritage.

Folk tales and the great story collections

India has a very old written tradition of story collections that draw on and feed back into oral telling. The Panchatantra, a collection of animal fables framed as lessons for princes, was translated into Middle Persian, Arabic and later many European languages. The Jataka tales of the Buddha's previous births, preserved in Pali, contain many popular stories. Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara, composed in Sanskrit in Kashmir in the 11th century, is a vast collection of interlinked tales.

Oral telling never depended on these texts, though. Every region has its own trickster tales, stories of clever women, ghost stories and tales of local heroes. Collections made in the 19th and 20th centuries, such as Lal Behari Day's Folk-Tales of Bengal (1883), and A. K. Ramanujan's Folktales from India (1991), which gathered tales from many Indian languages, give a good sense of this variety.

Oral epics and the performers who carry them

Some of the most remarkable Indian folklore takes the form of long oral epics, sung or recited over many nights by trained performers. These are performance traditions, often with music, scroll paintings or dance, and they are learnt by apprenticeship within families or communities.

  • Pabuji ki Phad, Rajasthan: the epic of the folk hero Pabuji, sung by bhopa performers in front of a long painted cloth scroll called a phad, lit by a lamp at night.
  • Alha, Bundelkhand and the Gangetic plain: the ballad of the warrior brothers Alha and Udal, sung loudly and often during the rainy season.
  • Pandavani, Chhattisgarh: episodes from the Mahabharata told by a single performer with a tambura, made widely known by Teejan Bai.
  • Lorikayan, Bhojpuri and Magahi regions: the long epic of the cowherd hero Lorik.
  • Burra katha, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana: a storyteller with a drum and two companions, used for epics and, in the 20th century, for social messages.
  • Theyyam, north Kerala: a ritual performance in which performers embody local deities and heroes, treated here as a social and historical practice.

Songs, proverbs and everyday folklore

Most folklore is less formal than the great epics. Work songs accompany sowing and harvesting, wedding songs tease the groom's family, lullabies and women's songs carry family histories, and festival songs mark the seasons. The Baul singers of Bengal, recognised by UNESCO in 2005 as part of the intangible heritage of humanity, are a well-known example of a song tradition with its own philosophy.

Proverbs and riddles are compact folklore. They carry practical knowledge about weather, farming and human nature, and they are excellent sources for studying language. Many tribal communities maintain their own oral literature in languages with little or no written tradition, which makes recording it, with the community's consent, an important task.

How folklorists study Indian folklore

Early collectors in the 19th century, often missionaries and colonial officers, wrote tales down and translated them, sometimes with heavy editing. Later scholars such as Verrier Elwin in central India, Devendra Satyarthi who collected folk songs across the country, and Komal Kothari who documented the oral traditions of Rajasthan, paid more attention to performers and context. Scholars use tale-type and motif indexes to compare stories across cultures, and anthropologists use ethnography to understand who tells which stories, to whom and why.

Today the focus is on performance and community. A story's meaning depends on who is telling it, the audience, the occasion and the music, so folklorists record full performances with audio and video, and work with performers as experts. The oral history and neighbourhood memory lab teaches the basic recording and interviewing skills this work needs.

Where to experience Indian folklore

Museums that work closely with communities are a good way in. The Bhopal Tribal Museum presents the stories, ritual art and homes of communities from Madhya Pradesh, much of it made by artists from those communities. The National Crafts Museum in Delhi shows how story and craft come together in painted scrolls, puppets and textiles. Rock art is a much older form of visual storytelling, explored in our rock art of India lecture.

If you want to work with stories yourself, the heritage podcast and storytelling studio helps students turn recorded memories and tales into short audio pieces, with attention to accuracy and consent.

How we run this

  • Schools: an oral history lab where students record stories from their own families and neighbourhood.
  • Colleges and clubs: a heritage podcast and storytelling studio for turning recordings into audio pieces.
  • Museum groups: guided visits to the Bhopal Tribal Museum or the National Crafts Museum in Delhi.

Questions people ask

What is folklore in simple words?

Folklore is the traditional knowledge and art that people pass on informally, by word of mouth and example. It includes folk tales, songs, proverbs, riddles, festivals, games, crafts and customs. It changes a little each time it is passed on, so there is rarely one correct version.

What are some famous Indian folk tales?

Well-known collections include the Panchatantra animal fables, the Jataka tales of the Buddha's previous births and Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara. Popular oral tales include stories of Tenali Rama and Birbal, and countless regional trickster, ghost and hero tales collected in works such as A. K. Ramanujan's Folktales from India.

What is Pabuji ki Phad?

Pabuji ki Phad is an oral epic tradition of Rajasthan. Bhopa performers sing the story of the folk hero Pabuji at night in front of a long painted cloth scroll called a phad, pointing to scenes as the story unfolds. It combines singing, music, painting and ritual.

What is the difference between folklore and mythology?

Mythology usually refers to sacred narratives about gods, the creation of the world and the origins of things, often preserved in texts. Folklore is a wider term for all traditional, informally transmitted culture, including tales, songs, jokes, customs and crafts. Myths can be part of folklore when they circulate orally.
